policy: The visible stars of X-ray and gamma-ray binaries, of Gaia BH2 and of pulsars with a recorded optical counterpart or a main-sequence companion in the compact-remnant overlay, with each value from the cited paper. A value stays empty when no individual measurement was verified; none is inferred from a mass ratio. Very low-mass, ablated black-widow companions are classed as brown dwarfs.

companions.note: A low-luminosity, slightly metal-poor red giant enhanced in alpha elements; it reveals the unseen black hole through its orbit.
A K-type donor star feeding the black hole; the 4600 K temperature is the value adopted in the mass analysis.
A cool dwarf donor; its K7 V to M1 V spectral type is from near-infrared spectroscopy (Khargharia et al. 2013, https://arxiv.org/abs/1211.2786).
The blue supergiant HDE 226868, whose wind feeds the black hole; the published mass interval is +7.7/-7.1 M_sun and the larger side is stored.

A K-type giant losing gas to the black hole; its spectral type is from near-infrared spectroscopy (Khargharia et al. 2010, https://arxiv.org/abs/1004.5358). A wider third star also belongs to the system.
A small M-type donor; its M1 spectral type is from Gelino & Harrison 2003, https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0308490.
A K-type dwarf donor, as listed by Casares & Jonker 2014, https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.5118.
A subgiant donor. Its temperature is about 4200 K at the system's distance; the published lower limit is 4200 K.
A low-mass donor star, first caught through narrow emission lines from its X-ray-lit face (Steeghs & Casares 2002, https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0107343).
A spotted K-type dwarf with 0.1755 times the neutron star's mass; K4 V and 4500 K are from González Hernández et al. 2005, as cited.
The blue supergiant HD 77581, whose wind feeds the neutron star (Kretschmar et al. 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.13148).
The Be star that gives the system its name. Its mass is the midpoint of the 13-20 M_sun range the source lists.
A Be star whose gas disk feeds the neutron star's outbursts (Caballero et al. 2011, https://arxiv.org/abs/1107.3417); its spectral type is SIMBAD's.
A rapidly rotating B0 Ve star (Weng et al. 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.09423).

An evolved star at least 3,500 AU from the inner binary, 1.43 arcseconds away on the sky. Its evolved state dates the system to 3-5 Gyr; its plotted position is the system's. Its mass comes from isochrones.
A low-mass star that has fed the pulsar on and off; this is a transitional system moving between pulsar and X-ray binary states (Deller et al. 2012, https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.5670).
A low-metallicity star on a very long orbit, published as 2,000 to 20,000 years.
An optically bright redback companion with mean r-band magnitude 16.6 (Bellm et al. 2016, https://arxiv.org/abs/1510.00721).
A redback companion identified optically (Phosrisom et al. 2025, https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.06503).
An eclipsing redback companion. Its mass is the midpoint of the published 0.4-0.7 M_sun range.
A redback companion with long-term optical variability (Clark et al. 2021, https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.14849). Its mass is the midpoint of the 0.15-0.22 M_sun range quoted.
The companion of a transitional redback pulsar (Johnson et al. 2015, https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.06862).
A metal-poor “red straggler” in the globular cluster NGC 6397, from a high-resolution spectrum and Hubble photometry.
A companion in NGC 6397 that has probably just left the main sequence and begun transferring mass (Zhang et al. 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07880).
The Be star LS 2883, oblate from fast rotation: its equator is near 27,500 K and its poles near 34,000 K, with an equatorial radius of 9.7 R_sun and a polar radius of 8.1 R_sun.
The Be star MT91 213 in the Cygnus OB2 association.
A redback companion, studied with optical spectroscopy (Strader et al. 2019, https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.04626).

A strongly heated redback companion: its visible side varies from about 6900 K to below 3000 K across the orbit (Romani & Shaw 2011, https://arxiv.org/abs/1111.3074), and it has hot spots, likely magnetic poles, that move over the years (Kandel et al. 2020, https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.04105).
An F6-type star tidally distorted by the pulsar; the type is Linares et al. 2017 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.02232). The published mass interval is +0.22/-0.19 M_sun and the larger side is stored.
A heated companion of spectral type M1 or later (Halpern et al. 2017, https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.09511).
A He- or CO-core white dwarf identified optically at r = 23.33. Published intervals are +0.25/-0.19 M_sun and +1000/-800 K; the larger sides are stored.
The inner of the pulsar's two white dwarfs: hot and low-gravity, with log g = 5.82 ± 0.05. Its outer white dwarf has 0.40962 M_sun but no optical detection.
A low-mass white dwarf with a thick hydrogen envelope, bright enough for spectroscopy. The published interval is +0.007/-0.005 M_sun and the larger side is stored.
A white dwarf with a cooling age of 10.9 ± 0.3 Gyr. Published intervals are +0.13/-0.10 M_sun and +550/-470 K; the larger sides are stored.
A cool DA white dwarf; its radius scales with the assumed distance.
Probably a He-core white dwarf, matching the mass from radio timing.
A white dwarf with very low mass, whose spectroscopy set the system's mass ratio.
A black-widow companion: a very low-mass object heated by the pulsar and seen optically (Breton et al. 2013, https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.1790).
A black-widow companion: a very low-mass object heated by the pulsar and seen optically (Breton et al. 2013, https://arxiv.org/abs/1302.1790).
A black-widow companion irradiated by the pulsar, tentatively a heavily ablated very low-mass star (van der Wateren et al. 2022, https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.05872).
A black-widow companion modelled from its optical light curve (Schroeder & Halpern 2014, https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.7966).

The original black-widow companion, heated on its pulsar-facing side and cooler than about 2800 K on its far side (Fruchter et al. 1995, https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/9502084). The pulsar outweighs it 69.2 ± 0.8 times (van Kerkwijk et al. 2011, https://arxiv.org/abs/1009.5427).
